summary: Describes an experimental mapping between the standard Telnet network virtual terminal ASCII character set and the input conventions of the UCSB On-Line System. It is a short technical note for sites using that system over the network.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 570 describes an experimental mapping from network keyboard characters to keys in the UCSB On-Line System. Common keys map directly, while less common keys use two-character sequences and selectable modes.

questions: nvt ascii to ucsb on-line system mapping
how did rfc 570 map ascii to ucsb keys
subtitle: An experimental way to type UCSB On-Line System keys over Telnet.

tldr.problem: The UCSB On-Line System had more meaningful keyboard keys than NVT ASCII could represent, so network users had to type long sequences for some keys.
tldr.mechanism: The proposal maps common keys directly and uses an escape-character prefix for other keys. Modes and Telnet commands control how letters and line feeds are interpreted.
tldr.outcome: The experimental mapping aims to make network input to the UCSB system more convenient without requiring a special keyboard.

today: RFC 570 describes an experimental input mapping for network users of the UCSB On-Line System.

sections.title: Why a Character Mapping Was Needed
sections.content: Users accessing the UCSB On-Line System (OLS) over the network sometimes had to type several characters to specify one OLS key. The OLS keyboard had 168 meaningful keys, while NVT ASCII allowed 128 characters. A custom OLS keyboard could help, but the RFC presents a character mapping as a compromise between that hardware and long spelled-out sequences.
sections.plainLanguage: Some OLS keys required a long typed sequence because ordinary network keyboards could not represent them directly. The mapping offers a way to use existing keyboards more easily.

sections.title: Direct and Escape-Sequence Mappings
sections.content:
The proposal assigns one ASCII character to many frequently used OLS keys, including letters, digits, punctuation and operators. It uses a two-character sequence for other keys, with ESC as the first character. For example, the text specifies [ESC]? for the TEST key.

The meaning of letters depends on whether the user is in OPERATOR or ALPHABET mode. An alphabetic character after ESC is interpreted as if the opposite mode were active, allowing access to the other interpretation without changing the mode.
sections.plainLanguage: Frequent keys use one character, and other keys use ESC followed by another character. The active mode determines whether letters represent alphabetic input or operators.

sections.title: Modes and Telnet Options
sections.content:
The OPERATOR and ALPHABET commands select how letters map to OLS input. SHIFT reverses the interpretation of upper- and lowercase ASCII letters; UNSHIFT restores the default. INTERPRETLF and IGNORELF control the treatment of a line feed following a carriage return, which matters for terminals that send the pair together.

The RFC says the mappings fit within the earlier UCSB teletype-compatible interface and recommends labels on keys and a reference card for users.
sections.plainLanguage: Telnet commands let users select letter modes, reverse letter case and control handling of line feeds after carriage returns. These settings adapt the mapping to different terminal behavior.
